Turn a client brief into a presentation

Start with the decision the client needs to make. For a website redesign, outline the current problem, your proposed layout, what is included and the next step. Give Gamma the approved brief and ask for one main point per card. Review the outline before spending time on visual details.

Arrange the visuals around the message

Use one screenshot or example to support each important point. Keep text large enough to read on a shared screen. Compare the new layout with the source brief and check whether a reader can tell which work is included and which decisions are still open. For a presentation organized around a visual map, compare Prezi. For icons and illustrations, see IconScout.

Review the deck before sharing

Check product names, dates, scope and numbers against the source. Remove placeholders and test the deck on the device your audience will use. Confirm the sharing permissions and export format your client needs before delivery. The images on this page illustrate the workflow.

Choose the right format for your audience

A presentation for a live meeting serves a different purpose from a link someone reads on their own. In a meeting, you can explain why a number matters and answer questions as they come up. A self-guided deck needs enough context on the page for a reader to reach the same conclusion without you. Decide how the audience will use the deck before drafting it. That choice affects how much text to include, where to place examples and whether supporting details belong in the main deck or an appendix.

For a client proposal, write the decision in one sentence. You may need approval to move into design, a choice between two packages or confirmation of a deadline. If the audience cannot identify that decision after seeing the opening card, revise the introduction. You can still explain the background later. A presentation feels easier to follow when the audience understands why they are looking at it before they see a long list of details.

Build a brief before you generate anything

Gather the facts you want the draft to use. For a website proposal, that might mean the agreed scope, the main problems customers encounter, the pages included and the delivery milestones. For an internal update, it might mean the reporting period, three results and two decisions the team needs to make. Put these facts in a short list. Mark anything still under discussion so it does not appear as a promise in the deck.

Write the audience and purpose at the top of the brief. Mention what the audience already knows. If you are talking to the owner of a small business, explain technical terms in language they use. If the deck is for the team building the website, include enough detail for them to estimate or assign work. Keep the brief focused on material that can be shared with the intended audience and used with the service.

Then describe the sequence in plain language. For example, open with what customers struggle to do on the current website, show the proposed structure, explain the work and close with the approval needed. This gives the draft a beginning, middle and end. It also makes it easier to see where a generated card has wandered away from the subject.

Give each card one job

Think of a card as a unit the reader can understand at a glance. A card can establish the problem, explain a recommendation, show evidence or request an action. Put the claim in the heading and use the space underneath to support it. A title such as “Customers cannot find the booking button on mobile” tells the audience more than a title such as “Mobile.” It also gives you a clearer test for deciding whether the content beneath it belongs there.

When two ideas compete for space, split them. For example, put the new booking flow on one card and the schedule for building it on another. The first can show the steps a visitor takes. The second can explain how the work will be delivered. This separation helps someone who is interested in the design understand it without also having to read dates and dependencies.

After drafting, read only the headings in order. They should tell a simple story on their own. If two headings say nearly the same thing, combine the cards or give one of them a more specific job. If a heading introduces a new term, check whether an earlier card explains it. A quick heading review often catches problems that are easy to miss while adjusting colors and images.

Use visuals to answer a question

Choose an image because it makes a point easier to understand. A screenshot can show where a visitor gets stuck. A simple diagram can show what happens after a person submits a form. A comparison can help a buyer decide between two options. If a visual does not help the audience make sense of the content, leave it out or move it into supporting material.

Check how the image looks at the size the audience will actually see. A screenshot with tiny labels may be readable on your editing screen and impossible to read on a shared call. Crop it to the relevant area or show the detail separately. Add a short caption that explains what to look for. If a photo is illustrative, avoid presenting it as evidence of what has already been built.

Keep the appearance consistent from card to card. Pick one heading style, one treatment for captions and a small group of colors that remain readable together. Save stronger contrast for information that needs attention. On a light card, check that captions do not fade into the background. On a dark card, check that small type and image annotations remain clear.

Example: a six-card website proposal

The first card names the project and explains the decision. For a booking website, it might say that the business needs approval for a simpler mobile booking flow. The second card shows the current problem with a screenshot and a short note. The third shows the new path from the home page to the booking confirmation. These three cards establish why the work matters and what the recommendation looks like.

The fourth card lists the work included in the proposal. Keep the scope easy to verify. For instance, separate the layout changes from form configuration and testing. The fifth card explains milestones and what the client must supply, such as photos or approved wording. The sixth card closes with the action the client needs to take. If the proposal has an optional add-on, put it after the main recommendation so it does not confuse the approval request.

Prepare an appendix if the client needs detail about technical choices, analytics or performance targets. Each appendix card should answer a likely question. A client who wants to know how the booking email works can then see that detail without reading it during the main walkthrough. Before the meeting, practice moving between the main deck and the appendix so it is easy to find the right answer when asked.

Example: a monthly SEO report

Start with the reporting period and the decision your client needs to make. Pick the few metrics that explain what happened, such as clicks, impressions and conversions, depending on the goal you agreed with the client. Verify dates and totals in the original report. If the audience needs to compare two periods, give both periods the same scope and show the comparison clearly.

Make a separate card for the most useful observation. For example, if a group of pages gained impressions but did not gain clicks, show the relevant comparison and explain what the team will investigate. Present observations separately from explanations that still need testing. Then close with the next actions, the person responsible and the information that would confirm whether the change worked.

Keep detailed tables outside the main cards if they will be difficult to read during the call. You can offer them as supporting material for someone who wants to look up a particular page. Label the source and reporting period on the charts you keep. That prevents a screenshot of the deck from losing the context needed to interpret the numbers later.

Review the draft for facts and commitments

Read every statement that refers to a number, date, price or promised feature. Compare it with the brief. Watch for wording that makes an estimate sound like a commitment. If the project is awaiting approval, explain which items are proposed. If a deadline depends on receiving materials, put that dependency next to the date. A deck is often forwarded after a meeting, so the qualification should make sense even when you are not there to explain it.

Check whether names and terms are consistent. Use the same name for a package everywhere and make sure the links go to the intended pages. For images, check that a screenshot belongs to the correct version of the product. Give the deck to a colleague for a short read if you can. Ask them to state the main recommendation and the next step. Their answer will tell you whether the deck communicates what you intended.

Check sharing and exports before the meeting

Decide who needs to open the deck and what they should be able to do. A client reviewing a proposal may only need to view it. A teammate preparing the presentation may need editing access. Check the available permissions in your workspace and test the link from a separate browser session if appropriate. Remove client information from any version you intend to share publicly.

If the audience requires an exported copy, confirm that the format is available under your access option. Open the exported file and check charts, captions, spacing and links. An interactive card can behave differently when it is converted to a static file. Prepare the version you need before the meeting, rather than assuming that a link and an export will look the same on every device.

Decide whether Gamma fits your workflow

Start with a small project that resembles work you actually do. A simple proposal or weekly update is enough. Measure the work from brief to approved deck, including editing and review. The first draft may save time, but the important test is how long it takes to prepare something you can share confidently. Note whether revisions, branding and delivery are easy enough for the people who will use it.

If your team needs precise control of a fixed document or slide layout, test those requirements before moving a large project. If your goal is to prepare a structured presentation from an outline and share it with a client, focus on how easily the draft can be reviewed, edited and opened. Keep a copy of the approved text and important assets so that you can reuse them in another format when needed.

Frequently asked questions about Gamma AI

Can I use Gamma for a first presentation?

Yes. Begin with a short brief, an audience and a decision. Draft a small deck and review each card for accuracy. Put your strongest visual near the point it explains. Rehearse once at normal speed so you know where the audience may need an extra example or pause.

How much information should each card contain?

Use enough to explain one main point. If a card needs several paragraphs or a large table, split the material or move supporting detail into an appendix. For a deck shared as a link, give readers enough context to understand the evidence on their own.

Can I use the same deck for a call and a follow-up?

Yes, but review both uses. A call deck can rely on your narration, while a follow-up copy may need notes or captions that explain what was said. Check permissions and test the link after making the final changes. Clearly label any items that still need approval.

Where can I confirm plan details?

Use the Gamma order link on this page to review the listed terms. If your project depends on a particular export format, workspace feature or level of access, ask the SEOGBTools team before ordering. Test those features on a short presentation before using the service for a deadline.
